title: Ajrak makers and the language of apprenticeship
summary: Ajrak teaching moves between workshops and classrooms. Its continuity depends on recognising makers as teachers, with knowledge that exceeds a printed pattern.

body.text: An ajrak can be photographed in a moment; learning how to make one is a different undertaking. The finished cloth reveals pattern and colour, but not every decision that produced them. For an archive concerned with living heritage, the relationship between maker and learner deserves attention alongside the textile itself. A pattern catalogue cannot stand in for a teacher.
The maker as educator

In a small qualitative study published in 2021, education researcher Aruj Khaliq interviewed people involved in teaching craft heritage in Pakistan. One participant, Sindh artisan Muhammad Ghulam Abbas, described invitations to teach ajrak in educational institutions. The account places a practising maker in the role of an educator, rather than treating craft expertise merely as material for someone else’s lesson.

Khaliq’s discussion also considers learning through sustained guidance and the connection between craft and other subjects. It is a study of selected perspectives, not a national survey demonstrating how every ajrak workshop trains its apprentices. That distinction leaves room for different teaching arrangements and for artisans who do not work with formal institutions.

A British Council programme guide offers another specific example: it identifies Ghulam Abbas Soomro as a master block printer from Bhit Shah and describes engagement with textile and fashion education. This is evidence of a named practitioner’s educational work. It should not be expanded into a claim that every student encounter provides a full apprenticeship.
Demonstration is only a beginning

Consider the difference between watching a printed impression and learning to judge it. In a hypothetical teaching exercise, a learner might compare two attempts, explain where the repeat fails, and try again with feedback. The educational value lies partly in being able to recognise and discuss a mistake. A successful souvenir print, by itself, tells us much less about what was learned.

An archive interview could therefore ask who taught a maker, which tasks a beginner is allowed to attempt, and how competence is recognised. These are proposed questions, not answers supplied on behalf of practitioners. Local terms should be recorded with their speaker and context instead of being presented as a universal vocabulary for all Sindh workshops.
Recording without replacing

Noorjehan Bilgrami’s documented work includes the book Sindh jo Ajrak and the film Sun, Fire, River, Ajrak. Their existence shows that recording the craft has taken several forms. Neither a book citation nor a film title, however, authorises an archive to reproduce a maker’s designs or disclose workshop knowledge without agreement.

Good documentation should distinguish the teacher, the workshop, the person recording the lesson and the person making the object. It should also ask what may be shared publicly. A maker can welcome visitors while declining to reveal a technique or have a learner photographed. Respecting those choices keeps apprenticeship a relationship between people, not simply an attractive story attached to cloth.

title: Chiniot woodcarving: learning by making
summary: Chiniot’s woodworking knowledge is learned within a specialised production economy. Apprenticeship connects skill, responsibility and livelihoods beyond the finished furniture.

body.text: A carved panel can make Chiniot woodworking look like the accomplishment of one pair of hands. The learning behind it is less solitary. Skill is developed through correction, repetition and relationships with people who understand different parts of production. Looking at apprenticeship changes the question from how elaborate a finished object appears to how someone becomes able to make it.
A workshop economy, not one task

Martin Enzner’s study, published in 2013 after fieldwork in 2012, distinguishes fitters, jigsawers, turners, carvers and polishers within Chiniot’s furniture economy. Its interviewed workers generally remained specialists. A person skilled at carving was therefore not automatically responsible for every operation on a finished piece.

Among the fully trained carpenters interviewed, learning with an ustad was the reported route into the occupation; the respondents had not received formal vocational training. Training periods differed. Apprentices did not necessarily belong to the same social group as their teachers. These findings describe that study’s participants, not every present-day workshop.

This division of work matters when attributing an object. A shop name may identify its seller without identifying its carver. Likewise, the person who assembled furniture need not have designed or polished its ornament. An archive should leave room for several credits rather than choosing a single convenient author.
Learning also creates obligations

Enzner records the close involvement of teachers in trainees’ working lives, and the sale of work made during apprenticeship. The study also describes movement to other cities through skills and contacts acquired in Chiniot. Teaching was connected to earning, not isolated from it.

That relationship should not be romanticised. Learning opportunities and unequal bargaining power can exist together. An account of apprenticeship needs to ask about hours, payment, education and the ability to leave, particularly when young people are involved. Admiration for intricate carving is not a substitute for those questions, and historical research does not establish current conditions.

Imagine an interview organised around a practice piece rather than a showroom display. The maker could explain which cuts were difficult, what an instructor corrected and when the piece was considered acceptable. This is a proposed research method, not a scene observed in a named workshop. It would allow the learner’s judgement to enter the record instead of documenting only the master’s reputation.
From famous buildings to named makers

The official record for Gulzar Mahal associates its woodwork with Rahim Bakhsh and Elahi Bakhsh. Naming craftsmen changes the familiar palace narrative: patronage is important, but it does not exhaust authorship. Such names should be preserved without assuming that a present workshop descends directly from them.

Chiniot’s craft history becomes richer when a visitor can move between a remarkable architectural interior and an account of how working knowledge is acquired. The connection is not that every chair repeats a palace. It is that both invite careful attention to decisions, specialisms and people whose labour may otherwise disappear behind the finished surface.

title: Multani kashikari as living knowledge
summary: Multani kashikari survives through working knowledge, training and access to production resources—not through admiration for blue ornament alone.

body.text: The blue surface of a Multani ceramic object is easy to recognise before its maker is known. That visual familiarity can conceal a harder question: who is able to learn the work, practise it and sustain a livelihood from it? Kashikari is living knowledge because people continue making decisions with materials. A photograph of an old tiled building cannot answer how that knowledge circulates today.
Knowledge and access

Ayesha Aslam’s PIDE case study of Multan ceramics distinguishes workers’ vocational skills from owners’ access to physical capital. Its interviews describe learning within production settings and unequal opportunities to establish an independent business. Possessing a skill and possessing the resources to use it commercially are different conditions.

The study also records respondents’ accounts of knowledge being retained within families, including reluctance to share particular stages of production. Those testimonies reveal tensions around teaching and competition. They do not establish that every Multani family behaves alike, or that inherited knowledge necessarily prevents new entrants.

For an archive, the useful lesson is to ask more precise questions. Who taught a ceramicist to prepare a body, mix a material or judge a result? Which parts of the process are shared, and with whom? A general statement that the craft passes from father to son would erase the different answers that actual makers may give.
More than one setting for learning

The Skilling Pakistan directory lists a Government Institute Blue Pottery Development in Mumtazabad, Multan. That institutional entry establishes a named training setting, not a promise about current admissions, staffing or the availability of a particular course. Those details require a separate current enquiry.

Another form of evidence comes from practitioner presentation. Ustad Wajid Art’s workshop description outlines teaching that connects clay preparation, pattern, pigment, glaze and kiln work. It is the workshop’s own account of its offer, not an independently assessed qualification. It nevertheless shows how a maker presents ceramic knowledge as an interconnected process rather than simply a decorative motif.

These different settings need not be treated as rivals. A classroom can introduce vocabulary and observation; a production workshop can expose a learner to repeated decisions and consequences. Whether either arrangement is effective must be assessed with the people who teach and learn there, not inferred from the word traditional or modern.
Document the judgement, not only the result

A useful future interview might compare a successful object with a rejected one, if its maker agrees. Why was one retained and the other set aside? Which decision would the maker change? Such questions recognise practical judgement without publishing a technical recipe or appropriating protected workshop knowledge.

The purpose is not to turn every ceramicist into an anonymous custodian of the past. Makers may teach, experiment, restrict access, change products or leave the occupation. A responsible account gives those choices space. Multani kashikari deserves appreciation as work carried out by living people, with expertise and constraints that cannot be read from blue glaze alone.

title: Truck-art workshops and changing commissions
summary: Truck art changes through the relationship between skilled workshops and their commissioners, from transport owners to education campaigns and cultural exchanges.

body.text: A decorated truck is both a working vehicle and a commissioned surface. Its appearance is negotiated among people: the owner who pays, the workers who build and finish it, and the artist whose choices give it character. Thinking about these relationships explains change more usefully than searching for one permanent meaning behind every bird, flower or portrait.
The workshop behind the image

Associated Press reporting in May 2025 follows Rawalpindi painter Muhammad Ashfaq and describes a collaborative trade involving painters, welders, electricians and metalworkers. Clients’ preferences and budgets influence the result. This particular account reminds us that the finished vehicle combines several kinds of labour; it is not simply a large painting made independently of its structure.

An archive caption should therefore distinguish what it knows. Naming the painter does not automatically credit the people responsible for metalwork, lettering or fittings. Naming the owner is not the same as naming the maker. Where those roles cannot be recovered, an explicit gap is more honest than a single sweeping attribution.
When the commissioner changes

UNESCO’s 2019 account of its girls’ education programme describes trucks carrying educational messages through Kohistan. The campaign used a familiar public visual form for a specified advocacy purpose. Its meaning came partly from the commission and the words selected for it, rather than from a timeless code assumed to govern all truck decoration.

This example also calls for care with claims about impact. A programme report can establish what was commissioned and why. Demonstrating a change in school participation would require a different kind of evidence. An archive can explain the campaign without turning its aspirations into measured results.

In 2023, Associated Press of Pakistan reported a truck-art exhibition and student engagement in Langfang, involving Pakistan’s embassy and Phool Patti. Here the work entered a cultural-exchange setting rather than a transport yard. The change of setting matters: a classroom demonstration has different audiences, constraints and purposes from decorating a vehicle that will carry freight.
Adaptation is part of authorship

The Karachi Art Directory profile of Haider Ali describes work extending beyond trucks to other surfaces. Such a practice should not be reduced to the anonymous export of a national pattern. It belongs to an artist with a career and decisions about where and how to work.

These examples suggest useful questions for future workshop interviews. Who proposed a design? What changed during discussion? Which decisions belonged to the commissioner and which to the maker? A motif may hold a personal, devotional, humorous or commercial meaning in one commission without carrying the same significance elsewhere.

Truck art’s continuing relevance is not measured by how little it changes. Its makers respond to new patrons and settings while negotiating material and visual demands. Recording those negotiations gives a fuller account than treating every brightly painted surface as an interchangeable emblem of Pakistan.

title: Embroidery learned at home and sold in markets
summary: Embroidery can connect household learning to market income, but its value cannot be understood without the maker’s time, choices and position in the supply chain.

body.text: A piece of embroidery can move from a household to a market without carrying the name of the person who stitched it. Along that journey, an account of family skill can become a sales description while hours of work disappear from view. Understanding the craft requires attention to both learning and exchange: how someone acquires competence, and how that competence becomes income.
Learning does not happen in one way

World Bank research on low-income urban women’s work includes accounts of skills learned within families and the practical importance of work arrangements compatible with domestic responsibilities. Embroidery appears within a wider discussion of livelihoods, not as a single experience shared by every woman. Household learning can be valuable without making the household the only appropriate place for work.

A 2017 Balochistan Review study of home-based embroidery workers similarly connects craft income to household circumstances and choices. Its participants should not become a composite imaginary artisan whose story supposedly represents an entire province. Their evidence is strongest when its setting and limits remain visible.

For future documentation, asking who taught a stitch is only a beginning. A maker may also wish to discuss how she developed speed, learned to interpret an order, selected materials or decided which work to accept. These questions recognise judgement and experience, rather than reducing expertise to an inherited female instinct.
The route to the buyer

The ILO’s Pakistan’s Hidden Workers draws on research conducted in two Karachi locations in 2016. It examines home-based work within wider supply chains. Its local findings cannot serve as current national wage statistics, but they challenge the assumption that working at home means working outside an economic system.

WIEGO’s research also records irregular orders and intermediary relationships in home-based production. The existence of an intermediary is not, by itself, an explanation of every outcome. A useful account asks who supplies materials, agrees a rate, checks the work and bears the cost when an order changes or is rejected.

Consider a hypothetical embroidered panel sold for a known price. That figure alone does not reveal the maker’s earnings. Material costs, unpaid preparation, delivery arrangements and the division of payment would all need to be established. An attractive retail price tag cannot substitute for that information.
Make room for the maker’s account

A consent-based interview should let the maker decide whether to be named, photographed or represented through her work alone. It should also distinguish her words from a retailer’s description. A family connection may be part of her identity, but it need not be the headline of her professional story.

The resulting account can recognise pleasure, ambition and resourcefulness without hiding difficult conditions. It can also acknowledge that someone may choose another livelihood. Preserving embroidery should not mean asking its makers to accept any terms offered in the name of tradition. The craft’s cultural value and the worker’s economic choices belong in the same conversation.

title: Baltistan’s irrigation channels as cultural infrastructure
summary: Baltistan’s irrigation channels are cultural infrastructure: physical works sustained through water-sharing arrangements, maintenance and changing relationships with outside agencies.

body.text: In a mountain landscape, a line of water can explain a settlement more clearly than a monumental façade. A channel connects a source to cultivated ground, but its continued operation also depends on decisions about maintenance and use. Baltistan’s irrigation systems deserve attention as cultural infrastructure: they join physical construction to the organisation of everyday life.
Following water also means following responsibilities

Joe Hill’s 2014 research examines farmer-managed irrigation in Thurgu, Baltistan, alongside a separate case in Kargil. It describes systems that use gravity to carry river, spring or meltwater toward fields. Some include storage that holds water overnight for later use. These arrangements respond to particular sources and terrain; they are not one uniform design across the mountains.

The paper treats users’ work as more than clearing a channel. Maintenance, distribution, resource management and relationships with outside agencies all form part of the system. Water infrastructure is therefore both a material network and a set of practical responsibilities.

This perspective changes what a landscape photograph can show. A visible channel may indicate where water travels, but not who repairs it, how turns are arranged or what happens during a shortage. Those questions require local evidence. The presence of a wall or sluice does not reveal the rules attached to it.
Continuity without freezing the past

Hill compares early twentieth-century revenue records with later practices. The comparison identifies change as well as continuity. External improvement projects can affect institutions indirectly even when they appear to concern physical works alone. A new structure does not enter an empty social landscape.

A Rural Support Programmes Network collection of mountain adaptation practices offers another way into the subject. Its irrigation examples connect open channels with local management and recurring upkeep. The collection describes particular practices, not a prescription that every village must follow the same arrangements.

Calling these systems heritage should not imply that users ought to preserve every old material or procedure unchanged. Their purpose includes sustaining cultivation. People may seek safer, more reliable or less demanding infrastructure, and those choices belong within the history rather than outside it.
Reading a working landscape carefully

For a future field account, a useful starting point would be a jointly explained section of channel: where the water comes from, which land it serves and who is responsible for that stretch. Different users might describe the same system differently. Those differences should be recorded rather than smoothed into a single story of timeless communal harmony.

An archive should also resist assigning an ancient date simply because a channel looks old. Recutting, repair and replacement can make an operating system difficult to date from appearance. Documents and local accounts may illuminate parts of its history without establishing its origin.

Baltistan’s irrigated landscapes show that heritage can reside in recurring work as well as surviving fabric. The significant relationship is between water, terrain and people who keep a system functioning. Recognising that relationship makes the cultivated ground intelligible without turning it into a picturesque backdrop.

title: Hunza’s fort and the settlement below it
summary: The settlement beneath Baltit Fort asks different conservation questions from the monument itself: housing, services, livelihoods and the effects of visitors.

body.text: The view of Baltit Fort from Karimabad can encourage a simple reading: a celebrated monument above, an attractive settlement below. Conservation becomes more complicated when the lower part of that image is understood as somewhere people live and work. A house, a lane and a shop have requirements that are not identical to those of a museum or landmark.
A settlement is not a foreground

The Aga Khan Trust for Culture’s account of work in Hunza describes concern about abandonment of older settlement areas and construction spreading into cultivated land. Its programme connected building conservation with improvements such as services and paving. The aim was not merely to improve the view towards the fort.

This historical project account suggests a practical distinction. Repairing a roof and maintaining a usable home may protect heritage more effectively than preserving an exterior while everyday life becomes difficult inside. A visitor sees a façade briefly; residents encounter its performance through seasons and daily routines.

That does not mean any change is automatically beneficial. It means that assessing a change requires asking whose needs it meets. Decisions about access, sanitation or circulation have consequences that cannot be judged solely from a before-and-after photograph.
Benefits need to be examined

A 2013 Freie Universität Berlin evaluation considers the relationship between built-environment preservation and community development in Gilgit-Baltistan. Its Karimabad discussion connects tourism with shops, handicraft production and marketing. It also records the vulnerability of visitor-related activity to wider disruption. Conservation and tourism are related, but their relationship is not a guarantee of steadily rising income.

The evaluation describes organisations and businesses responding to demand, including efforts associated with handicrafts. These are observations from a particular period. They should not be repackaged as current employment totals or proof that every household benefited equally.

For an archive, the important question is distribution. A business near a visitor route, a household elsewhere in the settlement and a person making goods for sale may experience the same conservation programme differently. A successful monument project does not settle all three accounts in advance.
Looking beyond the silhouette

The UNESCO Tentative List identifies Baltit as a fort property. That recognition is useful context, but a monument description is not a complete social history of the surrounding settlement. Nor does tentative listing mean inscription on the World Heritage List.

A future neighbourhood account could follow one lane through its uses rather than treating it as a photographic approach. Where do residents need access? Which spaces are shared? Which buildings remain homes? These are proposed lines of enquiry, not claims made from an aerial image or a brief visit.

Understanding Karimabad this way need not diminish the fort. It places the landmark within the relationships that make conservation consequential. The richer story is not simply that an impressive building survives above Hunza. It is that preserving a prominent monument raises continuing questions about the settlement beneath it and the people whose lives do not stop when visitors leave.

title: Rock-art corridors of the upper Indus
summary: Upper Indus rock art records many acts of marking across a landscape. Inscriptions and images illuminate movement without making every maker a foreign traveller.

body.text: Rock art beside the upper Indus can make movement visible without drawing a complete route on a map. Images and inscriptions occur at particular surfaces, but their makers did not all leave the same kind of evidence. Some recorded names or religious acts; others left marks whose circumstances remain uncertain. A corridor is therefore a useful way to think about connections, not a single explanation for everything engraved along it.
Many kinds of encounter

Jason Neelis’s research presentation places inscriptions and rock art within networks of movement through the upper Indus region. It distinguishes major routes from smaller connecting paths and considers both local inhabitants and people passing through. This avoids the familiar shortcut in which every unusual image becomes the work of a distant traveller.

The written evidence includes several scripts and languages. Identifying a script can help frame a question about chronology or communication, but it does not automatically identify the birthplace of its writer. Someone could use a learned language without having travelled from the place most associated with it.

Images require a similar caution. A stupa drawing, an animal and an inscription on neighbouring rock may belong to different moments. Physical proximity invites comparison; it does not establish that all were made by one group or as a single composition.
Reading is an argument

Thomas Höllmann’s study of Chinese inscriptions illustrates the interpretive work involved. His discussion of a Haldeikish inscription proceeds from photographs and considers readings of names, titles and a reference to Wei. The name of a dynasty is not enough by itself to provide an uncontested date, because more than one historical polity used that designation.

This is a useful model for an archive caption. It should separate what can be seen, what a specialist reads and what that reading may imply. A proposed identification can be interesting without being presented as certainty. Translation should not erase the difficulty of the original evidence.
Sites, not an undifferentiated gallery

The official catalogue records locations including Hodar, Thalpan and the Sor Das group in Rondu. Keeping these names and geographic relationships distinct helps readers understand the distribution of evidence. Combining their images into a single decorative montage would conceal the individual surfaces and settings that make them informative.

The history of research also deserves precision. Karl Jettmar’s introduction acknowledges earlier knowledge of rock carvings before the systematic investigations begun in 1979. A modern research project should not be described as discovering a landscape that local people and earlier observers already knew.

For public interpretation, the strongest invitation is to look closely without intervening. Marks should not be traced, wetted or altered to make a photograph clearer. More importantly, the archive should preserve uncertainty in its language. Upper Indus rock art is compelling because it records many encounters across time; reducing those encounters to one effortless Silk Road story would make the evidence less, not more, remarkable.

title: Neelum valley: sacred remains and a river corridor
summary: Around Sharda, temple, fort and river setting invite a layered reading of Neelum’s landscape without turning sacred tradition into a fixed architectural chronology.

body.text: At Sharda, the meeting of watercourses helps explain why a small area can hold several kinds of significance. A temple, a fort and the surrounding settlement should not be read as one monument with one date. They belong to different histories, even where the same landscape brings them into view together.
A sacred place and its surviving fabric

The Department of Archaeology and Museums places Sharda Temple near the Neelum and Madhumati watercourses. Its record describes a raised stone structure and architectural details including trefoil forms. Such features give an account something material to discuss: position, construction and the organisation of the surviving building.

They do not, on their own, settle every question about origin. Architectural dates proposed for Sharda should be distinguished from the age of traditions associated with the sacred place. A story preserved in literature or devotion may be important without providing a construction inscription for the masonry now visible.

Published studies of the temple bring architectural description into conversation with its religious associations. Their value is greatest when those forms of evidence remain identifiable. An archive should not turn every statement about learning or pilgrimage into proof of an excavated university campus, nor use the absence of a particular surviving feature as proof that no earlier activity occurred.
A different structure beside the corridor

The official record treats Sharda Fort separately and associates it with the nineteenth-century Dogra period. It describes a construction using stone, timber and earth in the river-confluence setting. The fort’s purpose and fabric therefore need their own explanation rather than being appended to the temple as if both formed a single ancient complex.

Putting these structures on one map can be helpful. Giving them the same date or significance would not be. The relationship is spatial: different activities have occupied a strategically and culturally meaningful setting over time. Whether particular routes or institutions connected them requires evidence beyond proximity.
A river is more than scenery

Water offers a way to organise a careful reading without inventing a journey. The temple’s position, the fort’s setting and the routes available through a valley can be considered in relation to terrain. That approach does not require claiming that every historical traveller followed the same path or stopped at the same place.

A future field account should distinguish an observed present-day crossing from a documented older one. It should also record local names with their speakers and spellings, rather than assume that one transliteration captures every usage. These are practical safeguards against letting a smooth narrative outrun its evidence.

Sharda’s significance does not depend on removing uncertainty. Sacred associations, architectural remains and later military construction can each be meaningful on their own terms. Reading them together produces a layered Neelum landscape, provided the layers remain visible. Current access, permissions and travel conditions are separate matters and should be checked independently of any historical account.

title: The Margalla foothills before the planned capital
summary: Routes, caves and excavated structures in the Margalla foothills reveal histories that precede Islamabad’s modern plan and cross its administrative boundary.

body.text: The modern plan of Islamabad can make the surrounding foothills appear to be its natural frame. Their history is not confined to that role. Routes, shelters and archaeological remains belong to landscapes that existed before the capital’s streets and sectors. Understanding them requires looking across the present boundary between Islamabad and neighbouring Rawalpindi rather than treating that line as an ancient division.
A pass belongs to a wider route

The official heritage catalogue records remains of the Grand Trunk Road at Margalla Pass. The relevant record is geographically associated with Rawalpindi, not simply absorbed into Islamabad because the capital is nearby. This distinction matters for both mapping and interpretation.

A road fragment can help establish the material presence of a route, but it cannot demonstrate every historical journey later associated with that corridor. Road surfaces change, alignments shift and repairs accumulate. Describing a recorded stretch is more precise than assigning all movement through the hills to one unchanged ancient road.
Shelter, water and uncertain chronology

Shah Allah Ditta’s caves and spring provide another kind of evidence. Their combination encourages questions about shelter and water, but the official record should not be stretched into a detailed account of named occupants or uninterrupted use. Popular age claims need stronger support than their repetition in visitor descriptions.

An archive can be useful while leaving those questions open. It can identify the place and explain which features are recorded, then distinguish material description from religious attribution or local tradition. That separation protects the significance of the site from dependence on a dramatic but poorly supported date.
Excavation changes the questions

Ban Faqiran offers a different evidential situation. A report in Pakistan Archaeology describes excavations carried out between August 2015 and February 2016, investigating a stupa and a mosque. Their presence within the investigated area does not make them contemporary or parts of one original institution.

The stupa’s surviving masonry and architectural components provide evidence that can be studied through excavation and recording. The official catalogue also notes losses to its upper structure. A reconstruction of the complete monument would therefore be an interpretation, not simply a photograph of what survives.

These distinctions help explain why a landscape history cannot be assembled by lining up attractive sites and assigning them one era. Excavated relationships, standing fabric, documentary references and attributed traditions have different strengths. Each can contribute without being made to answer questions beyond its scope.
Before the capital, not outside its story

The point is not to describe an ancient Islamabad. That would project a modern city backwards onto places with their own histories. Instead, the foothills show how the capital now sits beside and within older patterns of movement and occupation.

A regional map can make those relationships visible while retaining accurate district assignments. The road, caves and stupa do not become interchangeable attractions. Together they invite a more attentive view of the Margallas: a terrain carrying several histories, not merely a scenic edge to a planned city.
